name: Rites of Spring
label: Dischord
lede: Fifteen shows, one LP, a four-song single, and a genre name they spent the next forty years refusing to answer to.

eras.title: Springtime for a stale scene
eras.text: By 1983 D.C. hardcore had grown bigger, meaner and more predictable, and a lot of the kids who built it had lost the thread. Three veterans of a hardcore band called Insurrection, joined by Eddie Janney from Faith, set out to keep the speed and throw out the macho pose.

years.h: Rites of Spring grows out of Insurrection
years.p: [[Guy Picciotto|f8200cea-b5e9-4145-b5a5-1d0838f2c288]], [[Brendan Canty|8b505ef0-c5a7-4deb-bc32-27c882f3c40e]] and [[Mike Fellows|58a7226f-e06a-4728-82a5-ddc4443025a4]] had played hardcore together in Insurrection. By December they're writing the first Rites of Spring songs: All There Is, End on End, By Design.

years.h: Rites of Spring, named for Stravinsky's riot
years.p: The name comes from Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, the ballet whose 1913 premiere ended in uproar. Guy Picciotto liked the double meaning too: a springtime for a D.C. scene that had gone stale.

years.h: Rites of Spring's first shows, and wrecked gear
years.p: Dischord dates Rites of Spring's first shows to spring 1984. They'd play only fifteen in all, each one like it might be the last, sometimes wrecking their own equipment on the way out.

years.h: Mike Fellows moves to California; Rites of Spring keep practicing
years.p: Bassist Mike Fellows heads west and the others rehearse without him, assuming he's gone for good. About three months later he's back.

eras.title: Revolution Summer
eras.text: For one season, D.C. punk turned outward and inward at once: benefit shows, protests at the South African Embassy, and bands singing about things hardcore usually shrugged off. Rites of Spring were at the center of it, with the record to prove it.

years.h: Rites of Spring · Dischord No. 16
years.p: Rites of Spring's only album, recorded at Inner Ear in February with Ian MacKaye and [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]] producing. Later reissues add the All Through a Life single and retitle it End on End.
years.xp:
Hardcore speed with the anger turned inward: confessional, melodic, and about the things punk usually kept quiet. The band pointed to The Smiths, Wire, the Buzzcocks and The Birthday Party, and to Faith's 1983 EP Subject to Change.

Critics have described the record as swinging between fast and furious and lush, but never losing its drive or its melody.

q: Punk is about building things, not destroying them.
years.h: Rites of Spring call a punk protest against apartheid
years.p: At the Chevy Chase Community Center, Rites of Spring use the stage to announce the first Punk Percussion Protest: punks with drums outside the South African Embassy, making noise against apartheid.
years.xp:
The embassy protests had been running since November 1984. The punk version came a week later, on June 21, pitched as noise loud enough to be heard inside the building. That night Rites of Spring played the 9:30 Club and Guy Picciotto thanked the crowd for showing up.

Rites of Spring's gear-smashing reputation followed them anyway, and at a 9:30 Club show Picciotto pushed back on it from the stage.

years.h: Amy Pickering and Chris Thomson name Revolution Summer
years.p: Amy Pickering, who worked at Dischord, and Chris Thomson coined "Revolution Summer" at a city summer-jobs office, as an inside joke about revolting against their supervisor. It ended up naming a whole season of D.C. bands.

years.h: Brian Baker says he coined "emocore" at a Rites of Spring show
years.p: On a bill with [[Dag Nasty|4709dd69-1034-4634-9e88-d1099453b192]], Rites of Spring and [[Embrace|9d1ad8e3-8740-429a-bdc5-52f96a9c4431]], Dag Nasty guitarist [[Brian Baker|1fd36abf-e43c-4b01-820b-d7280cc27ea5]] says he came up with "emocore" to make fun of the Rites of Spring set. That's his own account, told to Parade in 2025.
years.xp:
Baker said he didn't think of it as coining anything at the time. Only years later did a friend point out where the word had come from.

Whoever said it first, Rites of Spring never used it about themselves.

eras.title: Four more songs, then gone
eras.text: Rites of Spring ended the way they played: fast, with no speech. They cut one last session in January and split within weeks, and three of them were in a new band before summer.

years.h: Rites of Spring break up, under two years after their first show
years.p: Wikipedia puts the breakup in January 1986, right after the All Through a Life session; Dischord says winter 1986. No member has given a reason on the record.
years.xp: Fifteen shows by Dischord's count (Wikipedia tallies 19), one LP, and one single still unreleased.

years.h: Picciotto, Janney and Canty form [[One Last Wish|94f18045-7fe2-41df-bf24-0bed21c88eb8]]
years.p: Guy Picciotto, Eddie Janney and Brendan Canty start a new band with Embrace guitarist Michael Hampton. One Last Wish play out from August and record an album at Inner Ear in November.

eras.title: Same people, different names
eras.text: Rites of Spring was over, but its members weren't done with each other. In eighteen months they went through One Last Wish and Happy Go Licky, and then Brendan Canty and Guy Picciotto walked into Fugazi.

years.h: Brendan Canty becomes Fugazi's drummer
years.p: Brendan Canty replaces Colin Sears in [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]]'s new band, Fugazi.

years.h: All Through a Life: the last session, out after the split
years.p: Rites of Spring's final four songs, cut at Inner Ear in January 1986 with Ian MacKaye, came out as a 7-inch a year after the band broke up.
years.xp: The same year's CD and cassette of the LP folded these songs in, plus one more, Other Way Around.

years.h: Rites of Spring's four regroup as [[Happy Go Licky|4c18be5e-2e53-41a4-a4a1-d9080ff88f8c]]
years.p: All four Rites of Spring members, back together as Happy Go Licky and playing something much stranger: tape loops, sound effects, songs largely or entirely improvised. They never set foot in a studio.

years.h: Guy Picciotto starts singing with Fugazi
years.p: Guy Picciotto is on stage with Fugazi by their second show and joins for good once Happy Go Licky winds down.

years.h: Happy Go Licky's last show
years.p: Happy Go Licky, the four Rites of Spring members' later band, play their last show on New Year's Day at the 9:30 Club. After that, the Rites of Spring story continues only in Fugazi.

eras.title: Back out of the drawer
eras.text: With Fugazi drawing crowds around the world, a lot of new listeners went looking for where Guy Picciotto and Brendan Canty came from. Dischord gathered the Rites of Spring recordings onto one disc, End on End, and slowly let the side projects out too.

years.h: End on End: all of Rites of Spring on one disc
years.p: Seventeen tracks: the Rites of Spring LP, the All Through a Life single and Other Way Around, under the title most fans know. Dischord still files it as No. 16.

years.h: Happy Go Licky, finally on Dischord
years.p: Will Play collects live recordings from Happy Go Licky, the post-Rites of Spring band that never made a studio record.

years.h: One Last Wish's 1986, out 13 years after being shelved
years.p: One Last Wish broke up in January 1987 after mixing their album, and Dischord held it back. It came out in 1999, named for the only year the band existed.
years.xp: The album was recorded in November 1986 by Guy Picciotto, Eddie Janney, Brendan Canty and Michael Hampton. Dischord was wary of its growing reputation as a home for bands that no longer existed; one track slipped out on a 1989 benefit compilation.

eras.title: The word they never asked for
eras.text: By the 2000s, emo was a word on magazine covers, and Rites of Spring kept getting named as where it started. The band wanted none of it. Meanwhile the vault gave up the very first tape.

years.h: Mike Fellows releases an album as Miighty Flashlight
years.p: After years of session work around the Drag City label, ex-Rites of Spring bassist Mike Fellows releases a self-titled album as Miighty Flashlight.

years.big: A genre with their name on it. They never signed up.
q: I've never recognized 'emo' as a genre of music.
years.h: Guy Picciotto rejects the emo label
years.p: Asked about Rites of Spring being called the first emo band, Guy Picciotto flatly refuses the premise.
years.xp:
In a 2003 interview Picciotto said every band he'd played in was simply a punk rock band, and went further, calling emo "the most retarded term ever." His counterexample: nobody would say the Bad Brains weren't emotional.

[[Jenny Toomey|246fc8dd-a667-4a5b-868a-a5897bcd6c59]] put it plainly: Rites of Spring existed well before the term did, and they hated it.

years.h: Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder cites Rites of Spring
years.p: Rites of Spring had fans well outside hardcore: Wikipedia notes Pearl Jam singer [[Eddie Vedder|1a60d6dd-9d3e-40fc-a66d-3184f9ee0d61]] has cited them as an influence.

years.h: Six Song Demo, 28 years late · Dischord No. 176
years.p: Rites of Spring's first session, cut at Inner Ear in April 1984 with Ian MacKaye producing and [[Eddie Janney|323dd1dd-23e4-45ce-9aa9-c5492096d604]] newly on second guitar. It sat unreleased for 28 years, then came out on 10-inch vinyl and download.
years.xp: The tape holds End on End, All There Is and By Design, the first songs the band wrote, in their first recorded form.
